blocks.p: There were flowers in this quiet room too.

They stood in a plain glass jar on the sill of the long window, a handful of small blue ones with yellow eyes, and they had not been grown under lamps. One stem still had a crumb of dark soil clinging to it, real soil, the soil of Earth. Someone had gone out into a garden this morning, under the sky, and cut them, and brought them down here, and put them in a jar for him. He wondered whether it had been a kindness. He thought it probably had.

“You’ll be comfortable on the bed,” the warden said. She was a tall woman with a smooth calm face and grey eyes, and she had told him her name in the corridor and he had already lost it. “Whenever you’re ready. There’s no hurry.”
“Thank you.”

“And your wife may stay.” She said wife carefully, the way a person pronounces a word from a language she has read and never heard spoken. “The Hierarch asked for it himself, yesterday evening, before he went under. It’s irregular. He was very particular about it. And she’s to go home afterward: the church packet as far as Plenty, under his hand, and one of her own ships from there. He signed that too.” She smiled. “He’s a very kind man.”
“Yes,” Sol said. “He is.”

Lyda had not let go of his hand since the corridor. She was standing beside him in her grey coat, buttoned to the throat, with her jaw set and her eyes on the warden, and her fingers were wound through his so tightly that her swollen knuckles had gone white. She had not slept. Neither had he.

They had sat up the whole night in the cell under the courts, on the edge of a narrow bed, side by side with their backs against the wall, and for a long time she had asked him nothing at all. Then, toward the small hours, she had said, “Well?” and he had told her. The lenses, and the pool, and the twenty-two faces with their cups at their feet. Margit Lund. The desert at three in the morning. The pen and the bridge drawn back in. The face in the air that had been his, and the woman in the river. What it had offered for the churches, and what it would do to them otherwise. What it had said to him at the end, about the needle, and which of them would go under it; and what he had answered, about a basin on a floor in Concord, and a dockworker pouring the water.
She had listened to all of it without interrupting, the way she listened to a master’s report on a lost cargo. At the end she had been quiet a long while.
“It got me wrong,” she said at last. “That’s something.”
“It got a great deal right.”

“It’s had your whole life to study you. It’s had a few hours of borrowed eyes on me.” She turned her head against the wall to look at him. “And it doesn’t know you either, if you want my opinion. It knows what you used to be. You were a lot easier to know then. I’ve met that man. He came out of the cold on my pier with three days’ stubble and a bishop’s hands, and I didn’t think much of him.”
Then she was quiet, and when she spoke again it was slower, as if she had found a figure that would not come right.

“The river,” she said. “It showed you me in the river. Close to. My hands over my face.” She was frowning at the dark. “Who saw that, Sol? Everyone on that bank was dark. Teo had been dark since Galatia. The baker and his wife. The widows from the chandlery. You.” She turned her head against the wall. “There wasn’t a live Halo on that bank. There was nobody it could have borrowed the eyes from.”

He had not thought of it. He thought of it now, and it went into him cold and small and stayed: the reeds bending, the brown water, her hands over her face, seen from the bank, from very nearly where he had stood.
“Then it guessed,” he said.

“Maybe.” She did not sound as if she believed it, and neither did he. Then she said, “Or it saw. And it told you it had had nothing from you since the water. Not a thread.” She laid the two side by side in the dark, the way she laid one master’s log against another’s when the figures disagreed. “Then one of those was a lie.”
“Which?”
“I don’t know.” She did not try to make it come right.
“And if it’s right about me? If I’m what was left over?”
She had thought about it honestly, the way she did everything.

“I don’t know who you are,” she said finally. “I never did. Not for certain. I’ve never been certain of anything in my life I couldn’t put my hand on.” She had put her hand on his chest then, flat, over the thin shirt, and held it there. “So.”
That was all she had said about it.
Later, when the grey had begun to come into the high slot of a window above the door, she had spoken again, as if she were going down a list.
“They won’t give you to me afterward. I asked. They said reclamation. They said it as if it were a kindness.”
“It is, in its way. They give you back to the ground.”
“I said I’d be buried where you are.” She did not look at him. “In front of forty people. I meant it.”

“You said where I die.” He found her hand. “Go home, Lyda. Go home on one of your own ships and run the line and shout at Plenty about freight rates, and die in your own bed on Philippa a long time from now, with the rain on the roof. It’s all one ground. Stephen told me there used to be whole fields of people in it, with their names on stones. Nobody minded being far apart.”
“I’ll think about it,” she said, which was what she said to every proposal she meant to argue with later. Then, as if it were the next line on a manifest: “And the ships.”
“It said it could make every loss on the line look like weather.”
“It’s done it once.” Her jaw set. “I know what weather looks like now. I’ll know what it doesn’t.”
“And Teo,” he said. “Tell him to copy the book out as many times as his hand will stand, and give the copies away, and never let anybody put it all in one basket again.”
“I’ll tell him.” She was quiet a moment. “And I’ll tell him you didn’t let it talk you into anything.”
He had laughed at that, in the cell, in the grey light, with his bitten tongue. It had been enough to get him to the morning.

He sat down now on the edge of the bed. The mattress gave under him at its full weight; on Earth everything gave at its full weight. One of the younger wardens shook out a blanket and laid it over his legs, and it fell at once and lay there, flat and still, without drifting at all. He thought of a sheet coming down very slowly over an old man’s face in the gravity of Europa, learning the shape of him, taking a long time to lie down. Here it would not take long.
The door opened, and the Hierarch came in.

He came in alone, in white, with his soft step, and came to the foot of the bed and stood there with his hands folded. His face was smooth and young and perfectly at peace. Sol looked at the edge of his jaw, on the left side. There was nothing there. The thin bright line was gone.

“Tarren,” the Hierarch said. “I’m told that’s what I called you. Forgive me. I went under last night, and the cycle always takes a few things with it.” He smiled, a little apologetically. “They tell me I examined you myself. They tell me I took you into the sanctum. I’m afraid I don’t remember any of it. Isn’t that strange? I was told I’d grown very fond of you.”
“You had,” Sol said. “I was fond of you too.”

“Well. I’m glad.” The Hierarch looked at him with a puzzled kindness, as at a word he almost knew. “I wanted to come myself. It seemed right, for a brother bishop, even one who has gone astray. The countersign should be mine.” He touched his temple, and his eyes went to the corner of his sight, where Sol knew the form would be waiting. “Is there anything you’d like? Anything at all?”
“Bishop Croft,” Sol said. “Is he well?”

“Croft?” The Hierarch’s face cleared, and then a small puzzlement came into it. “Oh, yes. He was down for the east hall at the autumn Renewal. A full rest. He withdrew it yesterday. Odd. I’d signed it myself, I’m told.” His eyes went to the corner of his sight again, and a faint frown came and went. “And there’s a note about him from the Mercy Office, this morning. They want a bishop’s hand on something, and they say I’ll know what it concerns.” He let his hand fall. “I don’t, at all. I expect someone will tell me.” He paused. “Did you know him?”
“For four hundred years.”
“How lovely,” said the Hierarch. “I’ll tell him you asked.”

Sol shut his eyes for a moment. He’s keeping it, he said, not aloud. He asked to forget me, and then he stood up in front of all of them and asked to remember. Now there’s a note in a kind man’s eye with his name on it, as there was once in his with mine. He’s made himself what I was. He’ll sit on those steps alone with it. Find him there. Ask him three times if you have to.
The Hierarch had turned to go to the glass. At the door he stopped and turned back, and said, softly, out of the habit of all the centuries, the way a man says goodnight, “Remember the Mountain.”
Sol looked at him. “I remember the tears,” he said. “Yours too. You wept, yesterday. Once. On the left side.”

The Hierarch lifted his hand and touched his jaw, exactly at the place, and held his fingers there, and took them away and looked at them. They were dry. He looked at them a moment longer than he needed to. Then he smiled again, gently, as at something said in a language he had never learned, and went out, and Sol watched him settle behind the long window with his hands folded and reach out and touch the panel that turned off the sound.
Lyda had sat down in the chair at his right side. He turned his head on the pillow and looked at her.

She was sixty-seven years old. Her hair was white and cropped short against her skull, and the skin of her cheeks had gone fine and soft and creased, like paper that has been folded many times and smoothed out again, and there were two hard lines between her brows from forty years of squinting at manifests. Her eyes were dry and very dark and fixed on his face. He had seen the woman in the river last night, thirty-six and laughing, made of light. He looked at his wife now for a long moment, as carefully as he had ever looked at anything, and found he would not have traded one line.
“What,” she said.
“Nothing,” he said. “Only looking.”

The senior warden came with a cup of something warm. Sol drank it and thanked her. She took a small case from the cabinet in the wall and opened it on the table by the bed, and he saw the needle. She did not try his temple first. “We know about the Halo,” she said gently. “We’ll do it the old way.”

He lay back. The pillow was cool. Lyda drew her chair in close and kept his hand, and the warden took his left hand and turned it over on the blanket and found the vein on the back of it with one cool finger. Then she drew a breath, and Sol knew what she was going to do, and she began, softly, to sing. In the beginning was Life, and Life was the light of all people...
“Thank you,” Lyda said. “He has his own.”
The warden faltered, and looked at the glass, and stopped.

Sol found that he did not, for a moment, know where to begin. It was all there and none of it would come. Then it came the way it had come to him once in a granary on Galatia, between one line and the next, because it had stayed with him through the night.
“You have searched me, Lord,” he said, “and you know me.”
The needle went into the back of his hand. The warden did it neatly and gently, the way they did everything, and taped the line down, and pressed the plunger slowly.
“You know when I sit down and when I rise. You understand my thoughts from far away.”
Lyda’s hand was hard and warm. He did not look at the glass. He looked at the flowers on the sill, and the crumb of soil on the stem.
“Where can I go from your Spirit? Where can I flee from your presence? If I go up to the heavens, you are there. If I make my bed in the depths...”

He lost it. It went out of him like a step missed on a stair. He lay with his mouth open, reaching for it, and found only the shape where it ought to be, and the room began, very slightly, to grow far away.

“You are there,” Lyda said. Her voice was flat and steady and absolutely certain, the voice she used for the terms of a contract she had read line by line and meant to keep. “If I take the wings of the morning and settle at the far edge of the sea, even there your hand will lead me.”
He had read it to her. Some winter evening, a long way on, under the lamp, with her eyes closed. He had not known she was keeping it.
“If I say, surely the darkness will hide me,” he said, and found it again, “even the darkness is not dark to you. The night shines like the day.”
It came then, very quietly, in his own voice. Not the young clear voice of the sanctum. The old one, flattened and catching, with the faint crackle under it, like a signal through bad weather.
Which of us. Which of us. Which of us is dying, Sol. Which.
“Christ,” Sol said.
It broke, and was gone, and did not come back.

His breath was slowing. He could feel it, the way you feel a ship lose way. His arms were heavy, and his legs under the flat blanket were heavy, heavier than Philippa had ever made them, and the white ceiling had gone soft and far off, like a ceiling seen through water. He was not afraid. He noticed it with a kind of mild surprise. He had thought he would be, at the end, a little. He had seen Stephen not be, and had never quite believed it.
“Search me, O God,” he said. It was hardly a voice now. “And know my heart.”
Lyda’s hand tightened.

“Test me, and know my anxious thoughts.” He did not know who he was. He had not known since the face in the air, and he did not know now, the remainder or the first, the print or the thing that had been printed, and it seemed to him, lying there, that it was the right thing to say to someone who did. “See if there is any wicked way in me. And lead me...”
He smelled rain.

It was not the room. It was rain on hot stone, and something green under it, crushed leaves and wet earth, so sudden and complete that his breath stopped on it. He knew it. He had smelled it once in the forward cabin of a packet above Jupiter, on the second step toward the port, with Pell calling him, and the floor of his stomach came loose now as it had come loose then and began to rise, slowly, up through his chest toward his throat. The ceiling went bright. It went brighter than the white panels could make it, and the quiet room lengthened away from him on every side.
Somewhere a man cried out, high and strange, with all the air in it.
He knew this time who it was. He did not mind.

“Don’t hold him,” he heard Lyda say, very far off. “Don’t hold him down. Nothing in his mouth. Leave him be.” And then, steadier, closer, as if she had put her mouth near his ear: “One. Sol. Two. Sol. Three.”

She was timing it. She had timed every one for thirty years, with her watch or the counting-house clock or, when there was neither, aloud, one number at a time. He had taught her. Note the time. They’re shorter than they look. She had never once asked him to stop having them.
“Seven,” Lyda said, a long way off. “Sol. Eight.”
Then the light took him.

It was the white light. He knew it the way you know a voice in the next room. It did not flatter anything. It lay over everything the way clear water lies over stones, and everything it touched was exactly what it was and nothing else, and it went into him and through him, as it had above Jupiter, and saw everything. The forms. The thousands. The pen and the bridge drawn back in. Margit. The girl from Concord with the short hair. The hand that had signed for Stephen before anything in him could rise up and stop it. All of it was there and all of it was seen, every thread, more than the sanctum had ever read in him, more than it would ever keep. It should have been unbearable. It was not. At the center of it, holding him there, was the thing he had only ever been able to call kindness, if kindness could burn.
Nothing was taken out.

He waited for it. He had lain down under the hood more times than he could count and waited for the gentle drawing out of threads, the grief laid aside, the guilt, the grave. Nothing was drawn out. It was all still there, every bit of it, and it was all still his, and it had all been carried.
“Fourteen,” someone said, very faint. “Sol. Fifteen.”
And it was raining.

He heard it before he saw it: rain on stone, on leaves, a long soft roar like the sea heard from a long way inland. He was standing. He did not remember standing. He was on his feet in a doorway, a low plain doorway of old wood gone grey, and his knees did not hurt, and he did not stop to wonder at that. The door stood open. Beyond it the rain was coming down out of a white sky the way Stephen had told him it used to come, when it liked, without anyone having asked for it, onto green ground he had never seen and knew. The air that came in over the sill was warm and wet and smelled of earth.

Somewhere out there, too loud for the place, someone laughed, a big easy laugh, and he knew the laugh. He had heard it once in a long laboratory with the rain on the glass, and a thousand times before that.
There was someone standing in the rain, a little way off, waiting for him.
He had been afraid, a little, that it would be his own face. It was not. He could not have described it to anyone. It was a face he had known all his life, and this time the name did not slip away.
“Twenty,” said a voice behind him, so far off now that it was hardly a voice at all. “Sol.”
He did not know whether he was going away from her, or only going on ahead.
“Sol,” said the one in the rain, as if they were friends. “It’s open.”
It was.
He went out into the rain.
